title: Stacking Contexts: isolation, will-change, and GPU Layers
prerequisites: Understanding of the box model and paint order

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a pile of transparent folders on a desk. Normally, the folders pile up in the order you place them, and each folder's papers stay inside its own folder. A stacking context is a special folder that seals its contents: the papers inside can never jump in front of papers from other folders, no matter how they are shuffled internally. Once you seal a folder, the whole folder behaves like one single sheet when compared with the rest of the desk. That is what isolation does: it seals the folder so inner z-index battles cannot leak out.
progressiveExplaining.junior: A stacking context is a group of elements painted together as a unit, in a fixed order relative to siblings. It is created by positioning + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, mix-blend-mode, will-change, contain, and isolation: isolate. Inside a context, z-index only competes with elements inside the same context. To contain a sub-tree's z-index battles, use isolation: isolate on a parent — it creates a fresh context without needing z-index. This is the modern, predictable way to scope stacking instead of fighting z-index: 9999 wars.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, stacking contexts are the unit of compositing: each context can become its own composited layer (backing store) when it has a transform, opacity animation, or will-change. The browser's compositor then positions/animates that layer on the GPU without re-rasterizing the main-thread paint. Creating many layers increases GPU memory, so will-change should be used deliberately. A key correctness trap: a context clips the visual order of descendants to the context — you cannot interleave a child of one context between children of another, no matter the z-index values.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The rendering engine computes paint order via the stacking context tree: each context runs a background/border pass, then negative z-index children, then block-level in-flow descendants, then floats, then inline content, then z-index:0/auto positioned, then positive z-index children. Layers are promoted by the compositor when the element is 'composited' (transform/opacity/will-change/contain:paint, or force-compositing heuristics). The layer tree maps 1:1 with stacking contexts that were promoted; the main thread rasterizes each layer's content into a texture, and the compositor thread draws them with z-order. isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context without visual side effects, letting the subtree be promoted independently.

rosettaStone.react: React components wrap modals/drawers in a portal to a top-level stacking context, relying on the same paint-order rules.
rosettaStone.angular: Angular overlay/CDK portals mount to the document body to escape component stacking contexts for z-index control.
rosettaStone.vue: Vue transition wrappers often add transform for animations — which unintentionally creates stacking contexts; beware.
rosettaStone.svelte: Svelte transitions animate opacity/transform, creating stacking contexts and potentially GPU layers during the transition.

codeComparison.title: Fighting z-index wars vs containing them with isolation
codeComparison.summary: Global z-index escalation is fragile; isolation: isolate scopes the stacking battle to a subtree so inner values cannot leak outward.

legacyOrBad.label: Global z-index escalation
legacyOrBad.snippet: .modal { z-index: 9999; } /* ❌ OLD: global arms race — the next overlay needs 10000 */

modernOrGood.label: isolation: isolate to scope stacking
modernOrGood.snippet: .overlay-root { isolation: isolate; } /* ✅ NEW: fresh stacking context, no z-index needed */

interviewGotchas.question: Why does z-index: 999999 sometimes fail to bring an element to the front?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand that z-index is scoped by stacking contexts, not a global priority number — the classic production mystery.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: z-index only orders elements within the same stacking context. If any ancestor of your element creates a stacking context (position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, contain, mix-blend-mode, isolation), then your huge z-index competes only against siblings inside that ancestor's context. The ancestor itself is then painted at its own z-index among ITS siblings. So a modal with z-index: 999999 inside a transformed card is trapped: the whole card sits at whatever level the card's context has. Fix: move the element to a top-level context (portal/body) or remove the creating property from ancestors, or contain with isolation at a deliberate root.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'z-index is broken' or 'just use a bigger number'. Bigger numbers only matter within the same context. Another trap: assuming opacity: 0.99 or a tiny transform are harmless — they create stacking contexts too, which silently traps descendants. Candidates who trace the ancestor chain to find the context-creating property show real debugging skill.

interviewGotchas.question: How does will-change actually create GPU layers, and why is it not free?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the compositing model — that will-change is a promise that promotes the element to its own layer with real GPU memory cost, not a performance silver bullet.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: will-change tells the browser to promote the element into its own composited layer before the property actually changes, so the eventual animation (transform/opacity) runs on the compositor thread without re-rasterizing on the main thread. Each promoted layer is a separate texture in GPU memory, with its own compositing cost. Overusing will-change on many elements (or on huge ones) bloats GPU memory and can cause layer explosion, slow down first paint, and increase memory pressure on low-end devices. Modern browsers also auto-promote layers for running animations, so will-change is best reserved for a small number of known, imminent animations.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'will-change makes everything faster'. It is a trade-off: layers cost memory and compositing time, and an idle will-change layer keeps being re-rasterized if content changes. Another trap: thinking will-change creates a stacking context — it does (like transform), so adding it changes paint order and can trap z-index children. Candidates who mention GPU memory, layer limits, and auto-promotion show real understanding.
